title: Hybrid KV Cache Offload & Host Paging — draft design notes
content:
Context and motivation:

We are seeing KV cache memory become the dominant consumer on high-concurrency LLM serving nodes for several workloads (long-context chat, multi-turn agents). GPUs have limited high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and typical optimizations (quantization, layer slicing) only reduce per-token cost so far. Two complementary directions to expand effective KV capacity are: 1) offloading cold/less-frequently-accessed KV shards to host-attached storage over PCIe (NVMe or NVMe-oF) and 2) using host RAM as a backing store with cooperative paging between GPU and host (UMA/NUMA-aware). This doc collects a hybrid design and operational thresholds for experiments.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Extend effective KV capacity by 4–12x without regressions >5% in p99 latency tail for typical conversational workloads.
- Maintain deterministic worst-case degradation policies (avoid unbounded stalls).
- Provide knobs for per-customer policies (latency vs cost vs memory isolation).
- Integrate with existing scheduler/batcher and kernel pipeline so offload/prefetchs play nicely with batching windows.

Constraints and assumptions:
- Hardware: NVMe SSD on PCIe Gen4/Gen5, host RAM (NUMA nodes), GPUs with HBM that support explicit DMA/KV copy APIs.
- Kernel expectations: KV lookup path must be non-blocking inside the main token loop — we can allow async wait points (yield) but not synchronous stalls that block unrelated requests.
- Networked backend (NVMe-oF) may be used for Dedicated clusters; design should be modular.

High-level hybrid architecture:
1) Hotset in GPU HBM: exact, low-latency KV stored locally.
2) Warmset in host RAM (pinned or page-locked memory): ~2–6x HBM capacity. Access via PCIe DMA with low microsecond overhead. Host RAM holds compressed/quantized KV formats to reduce footprint.
3) Coldset on NVMe (PCIe): highly compressed/cold shards, prefetched asynchronously into host RAM on demand.

Key mechanisms:
- Shard-level placement: KV is partitioned into shards by token-range or attention-block id. Each shard has placement metadata (hot/warm/cold, last-access-ts, estimated reuse probability).
- Async fetch + fiber-aware yield: When a request needs a cold shard, the worker will enqueue an async read and yield its execution context to other fibers (we use the same lightweight cooperative scheduling used by batching). A max wait threshold (configurable) exists after which we either: 1) fall back to a smaller model variant, or 2) synthesize approximate KV (tiled zeros / cached prefix), or 3) serialize and wait depending on SLA policy.
- Two-level eviction policy: LRU+cost-aware for hot->warm, and LFU or approximated LRU for warm->cold. Eviction decisions consider estimated refill cost (PCIe latency + decompression time) and observed reuse.
- Prefetch heuristics: lookahead driven by sequence position, beam state, and recent access patterns. For chat, prefetch next-turn candidate shards when token position crosses configured thresholds.

Paging and memory semantics (UMA vs NUMA):
- On UMA machines (single memory domain), host RAM can be used as a straightforward backing store; pin frequently-copied pages with mlock when moving to hotset.
- On NUMA machines, maintain NUMA-aware shard allocation: worker threads pinned to GPU device prefer warm shards colocated with the GPU’s nearest NUMA node. Cross-node fetches are allowed but counted in cost metrics; scheduler will prefer migrating shards or remapping workloads when cross-node access exceeds a policy threshold.

PCIe transfer patterns and formats:
- Use batched NVMe read ranges for multiple contiguous KV entries to amortize command overhead.
- Store compressed KV on NVMe using a simple block header: [shard-id, version, compressed-length, uncompressed-length, checksum]. Compression options: LZ4 for low decode cost, Zstd-1 for higher density in coldset.
- DMA path: kernel issues a read into pinned host buffer, then issue a DMA copy into GPU pinned buffer. On supported HW, use GPUDirect RDMA or peer-to-peer to avoid extra copies.

Latency budgets and thresholds (initial recommended defaults):
- HBM hit: p50 = 0.2–0.5us, p99 <= 5us
- Host RAM (warmset) hit: p50 = 10–30us, p99 <= 200us (depends on PCIe gen and copy path)
- NVMe cold fetch to host buffer: p50 = 150–600us, p99 <= 5–10ms (varies by SSD and queueing)
- Max acceptable async wait before fallback: 2ms for low-latency customers, 10–20ms for cost-sensitive customers. These should be configurable per-deployment/tier.

Scheduler and batching interactions:
- Batching windows must account for expected warm/cold fetch windows. When a batch contains outstanding cold dependencies, we use progressive scheduling: serve rows that are ready while remote fetches complete for others.
- Kernel pipeline will expose an early-continue hook: if not all KV shards ready by token-gen time, attempt to generate tokens for the subgraph that is ready, producing partial output and scheduling re-gen if needed. This is experimental and requires model-level consistency checks.

Consistency, versioning and fallbacks:
- Shard versions: every placement move increments a version. GPU kernels reference versioned pointers; async fetches include version checks to avoid stale writes.
- Atomic promotion: warm->hot promotions must be atomic from the kernel's perspective. Use double-buffering of pointers and a short steal lock to swap pointers visible to generators.
- Safety fallback ladder: (1) attempt async fetch and yield, (2) if timeouts configured then try approximate generation, (3) if strict SLA then fail request (with monitored increment). Fallback policy is per-tenant.

Observability and metrics (must be exposed in Console):
- Per-shard: hits (hot/warm/cold), fetch latency histograms, compression ratio, reuse score.
- Node-level: host-RAM pressure, PCIe queue depth, NVMe IO wait time, cross-NUMA crossings.
- Request-level: fraction of batches affected by cold misses, time added to end-to-end latency by paging.
- Cost metrics: bytes transferred over PCIe, SSD reads per second.

Safety and resource isolation:
- Limit per-tenant host RAM usage with cgroups/limits. Set eviction aggressiveness per-tenant.
- OOOM mitigation: when host RAM crossing critical threshold, throttle low-priority tenants and aggressively demote warm shards to cold.

Experiment plan (short-term milestones):
1) Synthetic microbench: emulate KV hit/miss patterns and measure host-RAM fetch latency across PCIe Gen4 vs Gen5 machines. (2 weeks)
2) Prototype host-RAM warmset with pinned buffers and DMA copy into GPU pinned buffers; measure p99 paths and copy overhead. (3 weeks)
3) End-to-end cold-path: NVMe read -> host buffer -> DMA -> GPU for a toy model; exercise async yield and scheduler integration. (4 weeks)
4) Canary on Dedicated: run a small fleet with cost-sensitive tenants and track p99 and cost deltas. (6 weeks)

Open questions / design trade-offs to decide early:
- How aggressive should prefetch be for multi-turn chat where reuse is high versus single-shot generation where prefetch can waste IO? Suggest exposing a per-model workload profile and letting Optimize suggest defaults.
- Compression algorithm tradeoffs: LZ4 decode is cheap but gives less compression; Zstd better density but decode cost may hurt latency. We should experiment with mixed levels per shard.
- Kernel-level partial generation semantics are powerful but risky; consider disabled-by-default feature flag until validated.

Next steps (action items):
- Spike 1 owner: Miguel — benchmark NVMe->host->GPU DMA path, provide microbench numbers for both Gen4 and Gen5 hardware.
- Scheduler integration spike: Rae — wire a yield/resume hook into the cooperative fiber executor; create a smoke test where one fiber yields while others progress.
- Policy/console integration: Liam — draft UI knobs and telemetry panels for per-tenant thresholds and eviction controls.

Appendix (notes from hallway convo):
- On some platforms GPUDirect can skip a host copy — big win if available, but fall back gracefully.
- For NUMA-heavy nodes, consider a background rebalancer that migrates warm shards to balance cross-node accesses during low-util windows.

This doc is intentionally exploratory. Please comment inline on the heuristics you think are too conservative or optimistic. We will consolidate and produce a formal RFC after the initial spikes.
